extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy/literary criticism; writers, comedians, playwrights and comic artists interested in the theory of the comic
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical/theoretical criteria for what makes something comic, drawn from Bergson's essay on laughter; intended to guide analysis and creation of comic effects in gesture, form, social ritual, and literary technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic contrasts with gracefulness / results from rigidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic arises where the soul's lightness (gracefulness) is resisted by matter, which petrifies movements and thwarts gracefulness; the comic partakes of rigidness rather than ugliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative point: the imagination sees a soul shaping matter; when matter immobilises the intelligently varied movements of the body and imprints permanent grimaces, the effect is comic. Use contrast with gracefulness (not mere ugliness) to detect comic potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gestures and movements are laughable in proportion as they suggest a machine
rubrics_metrics.description: THE ATTITUDES, GESTURES AND MOVEMENTS OF THE HUMAN BODY ARE LAUGHABLE IN EXACT PROPORTION AS THAT BODY REMINDS US OF A MERE MACHINE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect mechanical suggestion in repeated or stereotyped gestures (e.g., a public speaker's recurring head movement). The clearer the 'man-as-puppet' image, the stronger the comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and subtlety in suggesting a puppet in visual art
rubrics_metrics.description: A drawing is comic in proportion to the clearness and subtleness with which it enables us to see a man as a jointed puppet while still retaining the impression of a living being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The suggestion must be clear (we perceive a set-up mechanism) yet subtle (the person still appears alive). The artist's originality lies in imparting a special kind of life to a mere puppet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and automatism provoke laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: A repeated movement (a movement always the same) returning at regular intervals makes us laugh because we perceive a machine that works automatically—automatism established in life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for periodic repetition (gestural, verbal, or situational) that halts the perception of living change. Repetition that is expected by the audience invites laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation exposes mechanical uniformity and increases laughability
rubrics_metrics.description: Gestures that were not previously laughable become so when imitated, because imitation brings out the element of automatism and mechanical uniformity hidden in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody and imitation are effective when they reveal the mechanical, repeatable aspects of someone’s behavior. Imitation functions as a diagnostic: it shows what is imitable (i.e., mechanical) in a person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deflecting gestures toward a simple mechanical occupation heightens the comic
rubrics_metrics.description: When a gesture is connected (without altering its form) to some mechanical occupation (e.g., sawing wood, striking an anvil), it seems more frankly mechanical and thus funnier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody devices should try to suggest a concrete mechanical operation correlated with a gesture to strengthen the puppet/machine reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity and multiplicity (likeness and unison) produce marionette imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Two faces that are alike, or several characters moving/gesticulating in absolute uniformity, give the impression of copies or marionettes, provoking laughter by suggesting manufacturing or invisible threads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage devices that synchronise actors or multiply likenesses intensify the hallucination of manufactured sameness and enhance the comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic/comedic devices derive force from revealing a clockwork arrangement while preserving plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodical repetition, systematic inversion of parts, geometrical development of misunderstandings, etc., draw their comic force from presenting an obvious clockwork arrangement of human events while retaining an outward aspect of probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights and comedians should aim to show an underlying mechanism (the 'clockwork') but keep enough plausibility to avoid breaking the audience's suspension of disbelief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguise and discontinuity revive latent comic qualities of fashion and custom
rubrics_metrics.description: A garment or fashion can be laughable when discontinuity (an eccentric or outdated dress) makes us distinguish the clothing from the person and see it as a disguise; continuity/custom deadens the comic quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To expose comic potential in fashion, introduce a break with customary continuity so the observer notices the incongruity between cover and covered (e.g., top hat on anachronistic head).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative logic treats inherent traits as disguise (transfer of comic quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination may treat innate features (a black face, a red nose) as if artificially applied—'painted'—so that the notion of disguise passes on comic quality even when no disguise objectively exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise when perception treats natural attributes as masks; this imaginative misreading can be exploited or critiqued. (Be aware of ethical pitfalls in applying such observations to real people.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisation of nature (artificial nature) is comic
rubrics_metrics.description: A nature that is mechanically tampered with (artificial waterfalls, contrived glaciers, artificially coloured flowers) suggests masquerade and can be a rich comic theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strengthen comic effect by contrasting the mechanically altered nature with the untouched original; satire often uses exaggerated artificiality (e.g., Jerome K. Jerome, Tartarin) as a comic device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation of ceremony/formula from matter renders social ritual comic (official automatism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceremonial and formulaic actions become comic when attention is fixed on their form rather than their substantive purpose, making participants appear like puppets performing a ready-made frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: customs officers asking 'anything to declare' of shipwrecked people; an MP treating a murder as a breach of company rules. Satire of bureaucracy benefits from focusing on form over function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of the artificial for the natural (administrative pedantry) is laughable
rubrics_metrics.description: When human regulation or pedantry usurps the place of natural or moral law—administrative enactments replacing nature—the result is comic, exemplified by characters who apply rules as if they were laws of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples of pedantry or professions treating their rituals as ends in themselves (doctors, lawyers) to demonstrate absurdity; quotes from Molière illustrate the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Any incident that shifts attention from moral/intellectual to the physical is comic
rubrics_metrics.description: ANY INCIDENT IS COMIC THAT CALLS OUR ATTENTION TO THE PHYSICAL IN A PERSON WHEN IT IS THE MORAL SIDE THAT IS CONCERNED. (E.g., a sneeze in a pathetic speech, 'He was virtuous and plump'.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot intrusions of bodily needs or accidents (sneezing, discomfort) into moments meant to display soul or character; such intrusions undermine seriousness and provoke laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner seeking to outdo matter — professions reduced to formality are comic
rubrics_metrics.description: When manner (form, ritual, professional etiquette) aims to oust spirit or matter, making the profession exist for its own forms rather than serving an end, it becomes a subject of ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirise professions by showing ritualistic adherence to forms (quotes from doctors/lawyers/judges). The more the means displace the ends, the funnier the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical defects act as overtones that complete professional or moral ossification
rubrics_metrics.description: A bodily peculiarity (stammering, slow speech) is an overtone that naturally complements and prepares the audience for the moral/intellectual rigidity the character will display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and actors often pair a physical defect with a moral foible to create a compounded comic impression; if the playwright doesn't supply it, actors may invent it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication/overtones: comic effects have related secondary notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic 'notes' (e.g., appearance triumphing over reality) generate overtones—related comic images such as the body tantalising the mind or manner displacing matter—that coalesce to strengthen the laughable impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating a comic theme, look for natural, instinctive overtones to layer on top of the central joke; duplicating types of ridicule (professional + physical) enhances effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: We laugh when a person gives the impression of being a thing
rubrics_metrics.description: WE LAUGH EVERY TIME A PERSON GIVES US THE IMPRESSION OF BEING A THING; transformation of persons into objects (balls, dummies) produces comic images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clowning examples: performers whose motions make them seem like rolling balls or wooden dummies. Use progressive staging (rebound, increasing rigidity) to produce the objectification effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual transformation / progressive suggestion technique
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic suggestion that a person is becoming a thing is often achieved gradually, by increasingly vague-to-definite hints—like hypnotic suggestion or the slow solidification of shapeless masses into objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective comic transformation uses a graded series of hints (start with real perception, then make it more indefinite, then definite). This technique underlies many coarse circus effects and can be applied in literature and stagecraft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm, rhyme and assonance can lull imagination to accept objectifying suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: By arranging rhythm, rhyme and assonance to rock the imagination between like and like, poets can prepare the mind to accept fleeting images (e.g., the image of a doll) and thereby create comic suggestion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary comic technique: use sonic and rhythmic patterns to soothe or hypnotise the reader/listener, making the subsequent comic image or transformation more readily accepted.
